---
title: "Concentration Imputation"
---

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
library(PKNCA)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
conflicted::conflicts_prefer(dplyr::filter, dplyr::select, .quiet = TRUE)
```

## Why imputation is needed

NCA intervals are defined by a `start` and `end` time. For AUC and related
parameters, PKNCA needs a concentration at the exact interval start. Two common
situations require imputation:

1. **No t = 0 sample.** The earliest measured concentration is after dosing, so
   there is no observed value at the interval start (time 0).
2. **Pre-dose sample.** A concentration was measured before the nominal dose
   time (e.g. a residual carry-over sample). The interval starts at time 0 but
   the only nearby observation has a negative relative time.

Imputation is applied just before each individual interval is calculated, on a
per-subject, per-interval basis. The original data frame is never modified.
The package's [Data Imputation vignette](https://humanpred.github.io/pknca/articles/v08-data-imputation.html)
describes the same mechanism from the implementation side.

### Example data: Theoph with t = 0 removed

```{r}
Theoph_df <- as.data.frame(Theoph)

# Remove the t = 0 observation to create a missing-baseline scenario
d_conc_no0 <- Theoph_df |> filter(Time > 0)
d_dose      <- Theoph_df |>
  filter(Time == 0) |>
  mutate(amt = Dose * Wt)

# No concentration remains at the dose time (the interval start)
o_conc <- PKNCAconc(d_conc_no0, conc ~ Time | Subject)
o_dose <- PKNCAdose(d_dose, amt ~ Time | Subject)
```

```{r}
# What does subject 1's profile look like?
d_conc_no0 |>
  filter(Subject == "1") |>
  head(5)
```

### Imputation in the automatic intervals

When `PKNCAdata()` generates the intervals itself (no `intervals` argument), each interval already carries an imputation method in an `impute` column (≥ 0.13.0): `start_predose_conc0` after a single dose, `start_cmin` or `start_predose` for a dosing interval, none for the back-extrapolated `c0` after an intravenous bolus, and only `start_conc0` (single dose) or nothing for sparse data. The `impute` argument of `PKNCAdata()` keeps its default of `NA`, which means "read the column named `impute`":

```{r}
o_data_auto <- PKNCAdata(o_conc, o_dose)
o_data_auto$impute
o_data_auto$intervals |>
  filter(Subject == "1") |>
  select(Subject, start, end, impute)
```

So with these data, a plain `pk.nca(o_data_auto)` already imputes a concentration at time 0. Passing a method string as `impute`, as the examples below do, applies that method to every interval instead of the column. The intervals themselves are described in the [Interval Selection chapter](intervals.qmd) and the [Automatic Intervals and Dosing Regimens chapter](auto-intervals.qmd). Before 0.13.0, the automatic intervals had no imputation. With `auto.interval.method = "legacy"`, which restores that behavior, these data give `NA` for `auclast` and `aucinf.obs`, excluded with the reason that the interval starts (at 0) before the first measurement.

---

## The built-in imputation methods

`pknca_impute_methods()` (≥ 0.13.0) lists the built-in methods with the names that imputation strings use, a one-line description, and their arguments:

```{r}
d_methods <- pknca_impute_methods()
d_methods$method
d_methods$description
```

| Name | String to use | What it does |
|------|--------------|--------------|
| `PKNCA_impute_method_start_conc0` | `"start_conc0"` | Sets the concentration at the interval start to 0, adding a row if there is none and **replacing** a measured value if there is one |
| `PKNCA_impute_method_start_predose` | `"start_predose"` | When there is no concentration at the start, shifts the most recent predose concentration (within `max_shift`) to the start |
| `PKNCA_impute_method_start_cmin` | `"start_cmin"` | When there is no concentration at the start, adds the minimum concentration observed within the interval there |
| `PKNCA_impute_method_start_predose_conc0` | `"start_predose_conc0"` | Keeps a concentration measured at the start; otherwise shifts a predose concentration there like `start_predose`; otherwise adds 0 (≥ 0.13.0) |
| `PKNCA_impute_method_end_conc_drop` | `"end_conc_drop"` | Drops a concentration measured exactly at the interval end from that interval (≥ 0.13.0) |

The four `start_*` methods act at the **start** of the interval; `end_conc_drop` acts at its end. You can inspect the signatures with `args()`:

```{r}
args(PKNCA_impute_method_start_conc0)
args(PKNCA_impute_method_start_predose)
args(PKNCA_impute_method_start_cmin)
args(PKNCA_impute_method_start_predose_conc0)
args(PKNCA_impute_method_end_conc_drop)
```

### `start_conc0` — zero concentration at interval start

Appropriate in a single-dose setting when no drug is expected before dosing.
The drug concentration at time 0 is assumed to be 0. A concentration measured
at the start time is replaced with 0, so a nonzero time-0 sample (3 of the 12
`Theoph` subjects have one) is discarded.

```{r}
o_data_c0 <- PKNCAdata(o_conc, o_dose, impute = "start_conc0")
o_data_c0$impute   # verify the impute string is stored
```

```{r}
res_c0 <- pk.nca(o_data_c0)

as.data.frame(res_c0) |>
  filter(Subject == "1",
                PPTESTCD %in% c("auclast", "cmax", "tmax")) |>
  select(Subject, PPTESTCD, PPORRES)
```

### `start_predose` — last pre-dose concentration

Appropriate in multiple-dose or steady-state settings where a true pre-dose
(trough) sample was collected just before administration. The method looks
outside the current interval for the most recent observed concentration. The
`max_shift` argument caps how far forward that pre-dose sample may be shifted
to the interval start: it defaults to 5% of the interval duration
(`0.05 * (end - start)`), or, when `end` is infinite, 5% of the time from
`start` to the last sample.

```{r}
o_data_pd <- PKNCAdata(o_conc, o_dose, impute = "start_predose")
o_data_pd$impute
```

### `start_cmin` — minimum concentration in interval

Appropriate as a conservative fallback: if no pre-dose value is available and
zero cannot be assumed (e.g. metabolite or endogenous compound), use the
minimum observed concentration in the interval as a lower-bound estimate.

```{r}
o_data_cmin <- PKNCAdata(o_conc, o_dose, impute = "start_cmin")
o_data_cmin$impute
```

### `start_predose_conc0` — predose if available, otherwise zero

Appropriate whenever you want a predose concentration used when one exists and
zero when it does not (≥ 0.13.0); it is what the automatic single-dose interval
uses. It also keeps a concentration measured at the start time, which matters
after an intravenous bolus, where that measurement is the C0 for the dose.
The [chaining section](#chaining-methods) below shows why the chain
`"start_predose,start_conc0"` does not do the same thing.

```{r}
o_data_pdc0 <- PKNCAdata(o_conc, o_dose, impute = "start_predose_conc0")
o_data_pdc0$impute
```

### `end_conc_drop` — drop a concentration at the interval end

The other methods add or change a point at the start of the interval;
`end_conc_drop` (≥ 0.13.0) removes a concentration observed exactly at the
interval `end`. It is meant for multiple-dose data where a sample at the
boundary belongs to the next dose, for example a post-dose concentration (or an
imputed C0) recorded at the time the next dose was given. Called directly, it
drops the 24 h point:

```{r}
PKNCA_impute_method_end_conc_drop(
  conc = c(10, 7, 5, 3, 11),
  time = c(0, 2, 6, 12, 24),
  end  = 24
)
```

In an analysis, combine it with a start method in a chain, such as
`"start_predose,end_conc_drop"`.

### The start strategies side by side

Running the four start methods on subject 1 (whose first sample is at t = 0.25) makes the
differences concrete:

```{r}
d1_conc <- d_conc_no0 |> filter(Subject == "1")
d1_dose <- d_dose |> filter(Subject == "1")
o_conc1 <- PKNCAconc(d1_conc, conc ~ Time | Subject)
o_dose1 <- PKNCAdose(d1_dose, amt ~ Time | Subject)
ivl1    <- data.frame(start = 0, end = Inf, auclast = TRUE)

auclast_with <- function(method) {
  res <- as.data.frame(pk.nca(PKNCAdata(o_conc1, o_dose1, intervals = ivl1,
                                        impute = method)))
  data.frame(impute = method, auclast = res$PPORRES[res$PPTESTCD == "auclast"])
}

bind_rows(auclast_with("start_conc0"),
          auclast_with("start_predose"),
          auclast_with("start_cmin"),
          auclast_with("start_predose_conc0"))
```

`start_conc0` adds conc = 0 at t = 0, while `start_cmin` adds the minimum
concentration observed in the interval (here 2.84 mg/L, the first sample) —
so `start_cmin` gives the slightly larger AUC. `start_predose` looks for a
sample at or before the interval start, and this dataset has none: it imputes
nothing, the interval still has no concentration at its start time, and
`auclast` is `NA` (the warning printed by the chunk explains why).
`start_predose_conc0` finds no predose sample either, falls back to adding a
zero, and so matches `start_conc0`.

---

## Applying imputation globally

The single-strategy examples above already used the global form: pass a method
name string to the `impute` argument of `PKNCAdata()`, and the same strategy is
applied to every subject and every interval — the side-by-side comparison
restricted itself to subject 1 only to keep the output small. With automatic
intervals, the string replaces the methods in their `impute` column.

```{r}
o_data_global <- PKNCAdata(o_conc, o_dose, impute = "start_conc0")

res_global <- pk.nca(o_data_global)
df_global  <- as.data.frame(res_global)

# auclast is populated for all subjects despite the missing t = 0
# (arrange by subject number — Theoph's factor levels are not in numeric order)
df_global |>
  filter(PPTESTCD == "auclast") |>
  select(Subject, PPORRES) |>
  arrange(as.numeric(as.character(Subject))) |>
  head(6)
```

---

## Chaining methods {#chaining-methods}

Provide a comma-separated string to apply several methods to the same
interval. Methods are applied **in order, left to right, each to the output of
the previous one**, so a later method sees, and can change, what an earlier
one did:

- `start_predose`, `start_cmin`, and `start_predose_conc0` only add a point
  when there is no concentration at the start yet, so after an earlier method
  has supplied one they have no effect.
- `start_conc0` sets the start concentration to 0 whether or not one is
  there, so it **overwrites** whatever an earlier method shifted or added.
  `"start_predose,start_conc0"` therefore always gives the same result as
  `"start_conc0"` alone.

To use a predose concentration when one exists and zero otherwise, use
`start_predose_conc0` rather than a chain. Three small profiles make the
difference concrete: one with a predose sample at −0.25 h, one whose first
sample is at 0.5 h, and one with a concentration measured at the dose time:

```{r}
d_conc_pd <- data.frame(
  Subject = rep(c("predose", "no_predose", "c0_measured"), c(7, 6, 7)),
  time = c(-0.25, 0.5, 1, 2, 4, 8, 24,
           0.5, 1, 2, 4, 8, 24,
           0, 0.5, 1, 2, 4, 8, 24),
  conc = c(2.0, 4.0, 6.0, 5.5, 4.0, 2.5, 0.6,
           4.0, 6.0, 5.5, 4.0, 2.5, 0.6,
           9.0, 7.5, 6.6, 5.4, 4.0, 2.5, 0.6)
)
d_dose_pd <- data.frame(
  Subject = c("predose", "no_predose", "c0_measured"),
  time = 0,
  dose = 100
)
o_conc_pd <- PKNCAconc(d_conc_pd, conc ~ time | Subject)
o_dose_pd <- PKNCAdose(d_dose_pd, dose ~ time | Subject)

auclast_by_method <- function(method) {
  res <- as.data.frame(pk.nca(PKNCAdata(
    o_conc_pd, o_dose_pd,
    intervals = data.frame(start = 0, end = Inf, auclast = TRUE),
    impute = method
  )))
  res <- res[res$PPTESTCD == "auclast", ]
  setNames(res$PPORRES, as.character(res$Subject))
}

methods <- c("start_conc0", "start_predose",
             "start_predose,start_conc0", "start_predose_conc0")
round(sapply(methods, auclast_by_method), 2)
```

The warning comes from `start_predose` for the `no_predose` profile, which has
nothing at or before time 0 to shift, so its `auclast` is `NA`. Reading the
columns:

- `start_conc0` puts 0 at time 0 for all three, discarding the predose
  sample and replacing the measured 9.0 at time 0.
- `"start_predose,start_conc0"` gives exactly the `start_conc0` column: the
  predose 2.0 that `start_predose` shifted to time 0 is overwritten with 0.
- `start_predose_conc0` uses the shifted predose concentration for `predose`,
  adds 0 for `no_predose`, and keeps the measured 9.0 for `c0_measured`.

Chains remain useful when a later method fills a gap rather than overwriting,
for example `"start_predose,start_cmin"` (use a predose sample, otherwise the
interval minimum), or when the methods act at different ends, as in
`"start_predose,end_conc_drop"`. `interval_add_impute()` (with its `after`
argument) and `interval_remove_impute()` edit chains in an interval table; see
[Editing intervals](intervals.qmd#editing-intervals).

---

## Per-interval imputation

Different intervals in the same dataset can use different strategies. Add a
character column of methods to the intervals data frame, then pass the column
name (as a string) to the `impute` argument of `PKNCAdata()`. The column may
have any name (≥ 0.13.0); a column named `impute` is also found when the
`impute` argument is left at its default of `NA`. The same setup is shown in
[the vignette's per-interval section](https://humanpred.github.io/pknca/articles/v08-data-imputation.html#imputation-by-calculation-interval).

```{r}
my_intervals <- data.frame(
  start  = c(0,   0),
  end    = c(24,  Inf),
  auclast = c(TRUE,  FALSE),
  aucinf.obs = c(FALSE, TRUE),
  cmax   = c(TRUE,  TRUE),
  impute = c("start_conc0", "start_predose_conc0")
)

o_data_per_interval <- PKNCAdata(
  o_conc, o_dose,
  intervals = my_intervals,
  impute    = "impute"         # name of the column to read
)

o_data_per_interval$impute
o_data_per_interval$intervals[, c("start", "end", "impute")]
```

`get_impute_column()` and `get_impute_method()` (≥ 0.13.0) apply the same
rules that `pk.nca()` does to find the column and the method for each row:

```{r}
get_impute_column(o_data_per_interval$intervals, impute = o_data_per_interval$impute)
get_impute_method(o_data_per_interval$intervals, impute = o_data_per_interval$impute)
```

```{r}
res_per <- pk.nca(o_data_per_interval)

as.data.frame(res_per) |>
  filter(Subject == "1",
                PPTESTCD %in% c("auclast", "aucinf.obs", "cmax")) |>
  select(Subject, start, end, PPTESTCD, PPORRES)  # start/end distinguish the two cmax rows
```

---

## Writing a custom imputation function

### Naming convention

The function name **must** follow the pattern `PKNCA_impute_method_<name>`.
PKNCA prepends `PKNCA_impute_method_` to the string you supply and looks up
that single function on the search path, so the convention is mandatory. A
function of your own is found this way without being registered, so it works
in imputation strings but is not listed by `pknca_impute_methods()`.

### Required signature

Modeled after the built-in functions:

```r
# Minimal required arguments (from args(PKNCA_impute_method_start_conc0)):
PKNCA_impute_method_<name> <- function(conc, time, start = 0, ..., options = list())
```

The function receives:

| Argument | Description |
|----------|-------------|
| `conc` | Numeric vector of concentrations for the current subject/interval |
| `time` | Numeric vector of times (same length as `conc`) |
| `start` | Interval start time |
| `...` | Additional arguments (must be accepted and ignored) |
| `options` | Named list of PKNCA options |

### Return value

A data frame with exactly two columns, `conc` and `time`, sorted by `time`.
It should include all original observations **plus** any imputed points.

### Example: impute with the mean of the first two observations

```{r}
PKNCA_impute_method_start_mean2 <- function(conc, time, start = 0, ...,
                                             options = list()) {
  # Only impute if the interval start is not already observed
  if (!start %in% time) {
    # Use the mean of the first two observed concentrations
    imputed_conc <- mean(conc[order(time)][seq_len(min(2, length(conc)))])
    conc <- c(imputed_conc, conc)
    time <- c(start, time)
  }
  result <- data.frame(conc = conc, time = time)
  result[order(result$time), ]
}
```

```{r}
# Use the custom method by its suffix
o_data_custom <- PKNCAdata(o_conc, o_dose, impute = "start_mean2")
res_custom     <- pk.nca(o_data_custom)

as.data.frame(res_custom) |>
  filter(Subject == "1", PPTESTCD == "auclast") |>
  select(Subject, PPTESTCD, PPORRES)
```

The vignette's [advanced section](https://humanpred.github.io/pknca/articles/v08-data-imputation.html#advanced-writing-your-own-imputation-functions) shows another worked example.

---

## When to use each strategy

| Situation | Recommended strategy |
|-----------|----------------------|
| Single-dose study; use a predose sample if there is one, otherwise assume zero | `start_predose_conc0` (the automatic single-dose choice) |
| Single-dose study, no pre-dose drug expected, any time-0 value to be ignored | `start_conc0` |
| Multiple-dose or steady-state, trough sample collected | `start_predose` |
| Endogenous analyte or metabolite, zero implausible | `start_cmin` |
| Intravenous bolus with a measured concentration at the dose time | `start_predose_conc0` (keeps it), or no imputation and let `c0` back-extrapolate |
| Sample at the interval end that belongs to the next dose | add `end_conc_drop` to the chain |
| Sparse sampling | `start_conc0` only; the sparse estimators refuse other imputed values (`pknca_error_sparse_impute`); see the [Sparse Sampling chapter](sparse.qmd) |
| Non-standard logic required | Custom `PKNCA_impute_method_*` function |

---

## Summary

- `start_conc0` sets the interval start to 0 even when a concentration was
  measured there; the other start methods act only when no concentration
  exists at the interval start time.
- The built-in methods are referenced by their suffix strings:
  `"start_conc0"`, `"start_predose"`, `"start_cmin"`, `"start_predose_conc0"`,
  and `"end_conc_drop"`; `pknca_impute_methods()` lists them.
- Automatic intervals carry their own `impute` column (≥ 0.13.0).
- Global imputation: `PKNCAdata(..., impute = "start_conc0")`.
- Chained methods apply left to right, and `start_conc0` overwrites what
  earlier methods did; use `start_predose_conc0` for "predose, else zero".
- Per-interval: add a character column of methods (any name) to the intervals
  and pass that column name to the `impute` argument of `PKNCAdata()`.
- Custom functions: name them `PKNCA_impute_method_<name>` and return a
  two-column data frame (`conc`, `time`).
